title: Lowering the voting age: practical lessons from Scotland, Wales and youth experts
label: 9 September 2026 · Modernising Elections
summary: Officials who ran votes-at-16 in Scotland and Wales, and youth experts, told the Committee that giving 16 and 17-year-olds the vote can work but needs time, clear joined-up communications, school and youth-sector education, and attention to ID and administrative burdens. They urged a cautious rollout with at least several months' lead-in, better data skills in councils, mock voting experiences, teacher training, and stronger media literacy for young people.

chapters.title: Introductions and context
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses introduced their roles and the Committee set the scene: votes-at-16 have been used in Scotland and Wales and the meeting will focus on lessons for England and Northern Ireland.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Good morning. Could you introduce yourselves for the record?

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: I'm Sandra Matthews from Powys County Council; I run electoral services and act as a deputy returning officer.

turns.speaker: Robert Nicol
turns.text: I'm Robert Nicol, electoral registration officer (ERO) for Inverclyde, East Renfrewshire and Renfrewshire, and depute convenor of Scotland's Electoral Management Board.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. My colleagues will ask questions about implementation, education and practical issues.

chapters.title: How Scotland and Wales rolled it out
chapters.takeaway: Both countries used a phased rollout tied to big elections, with benefits from a long lead-in, national messaging and dedicated engagement staff, but covid reduced the impact of early activity.

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: Wales started registration for young people on 1 June 2020 and then used the 2021 Senedd election — the Welsh parliament election — as the first big event. That gave time for registration, publicity and outreach, including a national leaflet and a household reminder before the vote.

turns.speaker: Robert Nicol
turns.text: Scotland used a 'young people’s register' for the 2014 independence referendum. Back then registration was more paper-based. The big lesson is: give officials time to plan. The Electoral Commission suggested six months; I'd say six months is the minimum to 'cover your back'.

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: Wales then added engagement officers and civic groups. Registration jumped substantially between the first and second cycle — in some places by 35% to 80% — once outreach was more active.

turns.speaker: Mr Dillon
turns.text: What channels did you use to reach young people?

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: We made short videos showing the polling station process, used youth groups and schools, and in Swansea they trained 'vote ambassadors' — students who encouraged peers to register.

chapters.title: Practical barriers: registration, data and resources
chapters.takeaway: Registration from age 14 helps but is often gated by parents, variable school data, and significant council admin work — automatic registration helps but has upfront data-cleaning costs.

turns.speaker: Dr Huebner
turns.text: An important point: votes at 16 means registration can start at 14, so the systems and schools need to be ready well before the first election.

turns.speaker: Robert Nicol
turns.text: Parents can act as gatekeepers: some won't register their child. That’s where education and trusted local voices help. Also, registers rely on up-to-date school data — term-time moves matter.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: You piloted automatic voter registration in Wales. How did that work in practice?

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: Powys used education records to find unregistered 14–18-year-olds and wrote to them. We identified about 3,000–5,000 people, but the data cleansing took a lot of time. Parents phoned with concerns about names on a public register. The opt-out rate was tiny, but the admin cost was significant.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: So 'automatic' looks easy for citizens but not for administrators.

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: Exactly. Year-one costs and skills in data matching and quality are the heavy lift. Over time it becomes more routine, but councils need those skills and resources.

turns.speaker: Mr Forster
turns.text: Would a big event like a general election risk breaking the system?

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: Yes — the volume and tight timings of a general election could strain a fragile new process. That's why time, resources and clear plans matter.

chapters.title: Education, engagement and young people's readiness
chapters.takeaway: Experts say 16 and 17-year-olds are capable of voting; success depends on high-quality citizenship education, teacher training, mock voting and youth-sector activity providing safe spaces to debate.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We now heard from the youth-focused witnesses. Is now the right time to lower the voting age?

turns.speaker: Leigh Middleton
turns.text: If not now, when? Young people keep asking for this. Politics affects their lives and they want a say. The issue is making sure communication and education reach them.

turns.speaker: Dr Huebner
turns.text: Research across countries shows 16–17-year-olds perform similarly to older voters on tests of choosing representatives. In Scotland public attitudes shifted to accept it once people saw it in action.

turns.speaker: Helen Blachford
turns.text: High-quality citizenship education from primary onward is key. We need statutory provision, teacher training, and practical experience — debates, mock votes, hustings — so young people can form and test opinions.

turns.speaker: Mr Dillon
turns.text: How do you avoid a postcode lottery in education provision?

turns.speaker: Helen Blachford
turns.text: Make citizenship statutory, fund teacher CPD, encourage specialist citizenship teachers, and use Ofsted inspection to ensure schools teach it properly.

turns.speaker: Leigh Middleton
turns.text: Also remember youth work outside schools: young people spend most waking hours out of class. Youth workers run mock elections, youth councils and intergenerational work that reaches those missed by schools.

turns.speaker: Sarah Smith
turns.text: Is there a risk that better-off kids will benefit more because of parental engagement?

turns.speaker: Dr Huebner
turns.text: There's that risk across the franchise, but evidence from Scotland shows inequalities in participation are smaller at 16–17, probably because many are still in school where they can be reached — so there’s an opportunity to narrow gaps.

chapters.title: Voter ID, misinformation and admin safeguards
chapters.takeaway: Voter ID and postal-vote ID checks create extra hurdles for youth; councils can issue voter authority certificates but process differences and ID lists may exclude some young people — media literacy and guidance for teachers are essential.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We heard about voter ID. What does that mean for 16–17-year-olds?

turns.speaker: Robert Nicol
turns.text: Voter ID isn't just about the polling booth. ID checks happen at registration and for postal votes. If a postal ID check fails, applicants must provide a passport, driving licence, or other documents — lists that many teens won't have. There is an attestation route (a signed confirmation) but it’s clunky.

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: Councils can issue voter authority certificates — a local photo ID for voting — but that’s a separate process and doesn't replace the government-prescribed documents for other checks. Young people need clear messaging and lead-in time to get the right ID.

turns.speaker: Andrew Cooper
turns.text: What about online misinformation and AI chatbots?

turns.speaker: Leigh Middleton
turns.text: Young people are digital natives but are exposed to lots of junk and AI-generated content. Media literacy needs to be part of the curriculum so they can spot bias, check sources and question sensational claims.

turns.speaker: Helen Blachford
turns.text: Media literacy is in the curriculum review and should be backed by teacher training. Teachers and parents need support too, because young people get news from Instagram, TikTok and message apps, not just BBC.

turns.speaker: Dr Huebner
turns.text: We also need reliable, trusted information sources aimed at young people and help for teachers on how to host safe, non-partisan political discussions in class.

chapters.title: Practical recommendations and closing points
chapters.takeaway: Give officials at least six months (preferably longer) to implement changes, fund data and staff resources, run mock votes, embed citizenship education and train teachers and youth workers — votes-at-16 can work if rolled out carefully.

turns.speaker: Mr Forster
turns.text: If you had to pick one practical reform to maximise participation, what would it be?

turns.speaker: Leigh Middleton
turns.text: Mock voting and real practice so young people know what to expect.

turns.speaker: Helen Blachford
turns.text: Access to high-quality statutory citizenship education and teacher training so young people can form and test political views.

turns.speaker: Dr Huebner
turns.text: Work to assist registration while broader automatic registration systems are considered — don't let young people fall through the gaps during the transition.

turns.speaker: Robert Nicol
turns.text: Minimum lead-in of six months is sensible; more time means less risk. Also, review all the ID checks across registration and postal voting to make sure young people aren't unintentionally excluded.

turns.speaker: Sandra Matthews
turns.text: Plan for resource needs: data skills, time for outreach, and clear, repeated messaging so young people and parents understand registration, ID requirements and voting options.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. That gives the Committee practical priorities to consider: time to implement, resourcing local administrators, better data, education and media literacy, and careful handling of voter ID.

turns.speaker: Helen Blachford
turns.text: ACT and I can help with curriculum and teacher training work if the Committee wants expert contacts.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We may take you up on that. Thanks again to all witnesses and members for a constructive session.
